item.title: Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
item.description:
Injured Australian lawmaker Helen Haines leaves hospital after alleged SUV attack
An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack has thanked well-wishers around the worldByROD MCGUIRK Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 1:18 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
MELBOURNE, Australia -- An Australian federal lawmaker who was almost killed by a car in an allegedly deliberate attack thanked well-wishers around the world Monday and revealed she had been discharged from a hospital where she spent the past month.
In her first public statement since being struck by a SUV on Oct. 19, Helen Haines said she was “very pleased to confirm” she had left Melbourne’s The Alfred hospital.
Witnesses said she was repeatedly rammed by the vehicle outside her electorate office.
The 65-year-old independent lawmaker said she would remain in Melbourne for the “rehabilitation stage” of her recovery. Her staff would not disclose where her rehabilitation would take place for privacy reasons.
“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.
“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across (my electorate) Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing,” she added.
Haines was in critical condition hours after she was struck when she was flown to Melbourne by helicopter from her hometown of Wangaratta, 236 kilometers (147 miles) to the northeast.
Surgeons amputated both her legs within a few days.
The hospital listed her as critical until Oct. 24 when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable. She had been listed as stable since Nov. 6.

item.title: A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
item.description:
A fire in a building in southern Thailand kills 11 people
A fire has burned through a building in southern Thailand and killed 11 peopleByThe Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:46 AM
Share
BANGKOK -- A fire burned through a building in southern Thailand early Monday, killing 11 people, authorities said.
The fire started around 2 a.m. in the building in Phuket that has a motorcycle rental shop on the ground floor and residences on the upper floors, officials of the local government said. It took firefighters about an hour to bring the fire under control.
There were 17 other people who were slightly injured.
Phuket police commander Surachai Sooksai said officers are still investigating the cause of the fire, but initial investigations found an electrical transformer near the building had exploded shortly before the fire started.

item.title: Kenyan farmers adopt new techniques to curb erosion during heavy rains
item.description:
Kenyan farmers adopt new techniques to curb erosion during heavy rains
Farmers in parts of Kenya are turning to simple soil conservation techniques to protect their crops and farmland ahead of the October-December rainy season that is projected to be heavier than usualByMAGDALENE WANJA Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:33 AM
LIMURU, Kenya -- After losing much of her farm’s topsoil to heavy rains two years ago, Elizabeth Itotia is taking no chances as Kenya faces the October–December rainy season, which is expected to bring heavier-than-usual downpours.
Itotia’s 5-acre (2-hectare) farm in Limuru, Kiambu County, in central Kenya, lies on a slope that makes it vulnerable to soil erosion. Catastrophic rains in 2024 washed away much of the nutrient-rich topsoil and destroyed several crops, including kale, spinach, cabbage, potatoes and native vegetables, leaving her with estimated losses of 200,000 Kenyan shillings ($1,500). More than 230 people were killed in the floods.
To restore the damaged land, Itotia and her family had to bring in topsoil from other farms, an effort that required additional labor and money to make the land productive again.
Her experience highlights the challenges farmers in Kenya face when extreme weather events cause losses. In a country where most farmers depend on the rainy seasons, recovering from such losses can take months or even years.
The Kenya Meteorological Department forecast El Niño conditions during the short-rains season, which runs from mid-October to December. The El Niño phenomenon is associated with warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. In East Africa, it can bring heavier-than-usual rains.

item.title: British women to receive automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
item.description:
British women to receive automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
The British government is pardoning women convicted of illegally terminating pregnanciesByBRIAN MELLEY Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:13 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
LONDON -- British women convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will be automatically pardoned Monday, the government said.
The action follows Parliament's passage last year of a landmark vote to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section from the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.
Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons and some will be issued posthumously.
“For too long, women have faced the devastating consequences of outdated abortion laws," said Heidi Stewart, chief executive of the British Pregnancy Advisory Service. “While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice.”
The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police had investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once “dragged from hospital beds to police cells” and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

item.title: Ethiopia and Sudan accusations of backing armed fighters as fears of conflict grow
item.description:
Ethiopia and Sudan accusations of backing armed fighters as fears of conflict grow
Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each country accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its bordersByFATMA KHALED Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:08 AM
CAIRO -- Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries.
Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.
In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the U.N. Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed.
Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement.
Each country denies the other's accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict.
Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.”
Here’s a closer look at what's behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region:
Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting.

item.title: Haiti revs up for elections as enrollment closes for candidates
item.description:
Haiti revs up for elections as enrollment closes for candidates
For the first time in Haiti’s history, three women have registered as presidential candidatesByDÁNICA COTO Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:00 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- For the first time in Haiti’s history, three women have registered as presidential candidates, joining 30 men vying to become the next leader of the troubled Caribbean country.
Next year’s general election is the first in more than a decade. The candidates include the widow of slain former President Jovenel Moïse, a respected economist, a well-known prosecutor accused of multiple summary executions and a former president accused of drug trafficking and sponsoring gangs.
Haiti hasn’t had a president since Moïse was gunned down at his private residence in July 2021 as part of a failed coup. Since then, Haiti has been led by various appointed prime ministers and a transitional presidential council that was dissolved in February.
Presidential and parliamentary candidates had until Sunday to register online. Haiti’s provisional electoral council is reviewing them and in January expects to publish a final list of names of those approved to run.
Haiti hopes to hold the first round of elections on July 18 next year and the second round on Oct. 4. Some experts question whether the country, which remains mired in gang violence, will be prepared by then.
Wolf Pamphile, founder and CEO of Haiti Policy House, a U.S.-based think tank, said nearly a million voters have been registered in the country of nearly 12 million people.
He noted that the government has set a benchmark of between 3 million and 6 million voters to hold what would be considered a legitimate election.
“That number is getting harder and harder to reach,” he said.
When the electoral process first began, officials were registering roughly 9,000 people a day. That has dropped to about 3,000 a day, Pamphile said.

item.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
item.description:
Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industryByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 9:25 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.
Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”
Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”
“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

item.title: Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as 'role models' on surprise Ukraine visit
item.description:
Prince Harry salutes wounded Ukrainian veterans as 'role models' on surprise Ukraine visit
Prince Harry has hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as role models, emphasizing the need for continued support from KyivByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 5:03 PM
Share
LVIV, Ukraine -- LVIV, Ukraine (AP) — Britain's Prince Harry hailed wounded Ukrainian veterans as society's role models Sunday and said they need to continue receiving support from Kyiv as he wrapped up an unannounced weekend visit to the war-torn country.
It was Harry’s fourth visit to Ukraine since the war started and his second time in the western city of Lviv to meet with patients and staff at Superhumans Center, an orthopedic clinic that treats wounded military personnel and civilians.
"We’ve invested in them before they put the uniform on and we must invest with them once the uniform comes off,” Harry said during trials for the Invictus Games, a Paralympic-style event he founded to inspire military veterans around the world to overcome battlefield injuries.
Harry, a British Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, watched wheelchair rugby players clash on Saturday and pickleball players — many with prosthetic limbs — compete to represent Ukraine at next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham, England.
The Duke of Sussex grabbed a paddle and teamed up with a player with an amputated arm as they competed against two men who had each lost a leg.
“I asked him to play and he didn’t refuse," said Oleksandr, a 49-year-old veteran from Odesa with an amputated leg. “He talks to people, he isn’t like a royal personage. He loves ordinary people. He is completely different.”
Harry hailed the resilience of Ukrainians and hoped the war would soon end.
“The rest of the world will continue to support you," he said. “In my mind you’ve already won.”

item.title: Rescuers recover last 2 bodies after methane blast kills 4 at a Colombia coal mine
item.description:
Rescuers recover last 2 bodies after methane blast kills 4 at a Colombia coal mine
Rescuers in Colombia have recovered two bodies from a mine, where a methane explosion left four people deadByThe Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 4:16 PM
BOGOTA, Colombia -- Rescuers on Sunday recovered two bodies that remained in a mine in rural central Colombia, where an explosion caused by a buildup of methane gas two days earlier left four people dead, officials said.
The country’s National Mining Agency in a statement on social media said search and rescue operations at the site had ended but an investigation into the explosion continued.
The bodies of the two other victims were recovered Saturday.
The mine is in Chita, a municipality in the department of Boyaca, about 149 miles (240 kilometers) north of Colombia’s capital, Bogota.
A statement from the Chita municipal government identified the site of the explosion as La Victoria coal mine. Security camera footage broadcast by Colombian media showed a massive plume of black smoke and flames rising from the blast.

The agency has previously warned that gases and dust can accumulate in coal deposits, creating hazardous conditions.
Mining accidents are common in central Colombia, where dozens of small-scale operators run coal and emerald mines.
The mining agency on Sunday reported the death of a worker at another mine in the department of Boyaca. The agency said the worker was trapped by a rockfall, but it did not provide additional details.

item.title: Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
item.description:
Thousands run Cuba’s Marabana marathon as many protest US sanctions
Thousands of people have run in Cuba’s Marabana marathon, using the event to protest U.S. economic sanctionsByANDREA RODRIGUEZ Associated PressNovember 15, 2026, 10:56 AM
Share
HAVANA -- Thousands of people ran Sunday in Cuba’s most important international marathon, with some using the race to protest U.S. economic sanctions against the island.
The Marabana marathon, held every November to commemorate the founding of Havana, took runners along city's iconic streets and landmarks, such as the Paseo del Prado and the Capitol building. Many wore signs expressing solidarity with Cuba.
“Cuba is not a threat; the blockade is,” read the signs that many of the 3,000 participants wore on their backs.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960, after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has endured decades of economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after U.S. President Donald Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba.
The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that disrupt water supplies and internet and telephone services.
“The blockade is suffocating the Cuban people," Yuraldi Cava, a 58-year-old state employee, said while running. “We are going to win this fight.”
Mayté Vigoa, Havana’s provincial government coordinator for sports, said the city had to make a major effort to hold the international race because of the island’s precarious economic conditions. She confirmed that the sportswear brand Adidas, a longtime sponsor of the competition, did not provide support this year.
